plan: Resubmit S002-01/03/05 (relabelled medium; S002-03 and S002-05 choices rebalanced to remove the length cue) plus eight new items with balanced choice lengths: inverted agreement, conjunctive-adverb boundary, modifier placement, concession transition, two-fact synthesis, predator inference, a weaken-the-hypothesis item, and sentence function.

passages.title: Historian
passages.text: Unlike earlier accounts of the mill town's decline, which blamed a single cause, the historian's new study is notably ______: she weighs several possible explanations and openly acknowledges the limits of the surviving records.

passages.title: Highway lanes (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some transportation planners argue that adding lanes to a congested highway reduces traffic. As evidence, they point to a widening project after which average travel times on the highway fell during the following year.

Text 2
Researchers who study "induced demand" report that when lanes are added to congested highways, travel times often improve at first, but within a few years the new lanes tend to fill as more people choose to drive, and congestion returns to roughly its earlier level.

passages.title: Library visits
passages.text:
A researcher compared library visits in three towns.
Town | Visits in 2019 | Visits in 2023
A | 12,000 | 15,000
B | 30,000 | 34,500
C | 8,000 | 10,400
The researcher noted that the town with the largest percentage increase in visits was not the town with the largest increase in the number of visits.

passages.title: Shipwreck dividers
passages.text: Divers spent three seasons excavating a merchant ship that sank off the coast more than two thousand years ago. Among the hundreds of objects they recovered from the wreck ______ a set of bronze navigational dividers, still hinged, which suggests that the crew plotted courses on charts.

passages.title: Bridge repair
passages.text: Engineers inspecting the Larkin Street Bridge found corrosion in both its steel cables and its concrete anchorages. The city's repair committee had expected the cables to be the costliest part of the ______ anchorages, which had to be rebuilt underwater, cost nearly twice as much.

passages.title: Botanical illustrator
passages.text: Trained as a botanist before she turned to illustration, ______ more than eight hundred plant species in watercolor during her expeditions, labeling each painting with the date and place it was made.

passages.title: Pedestrian bridge cost
passages.text: The new pedestrian bridge uses about 30 percent less steel than the design it replaced. ______ it is expected to cost more to build, because each of its curved girders must be fabricated individually rather than cut from standard stock.

passages.title: Songbird migration notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A researcher tracked two populations of a migratory songbird.
• One population nests in Norway; the other nests in Spain.
• Both populations spend the winter in West Africa.
• The Norwegian birds left West Africa an average of 9 days earlier than the Spanish birds.
• The Norwegian birds reached their nesting grounds an average of 11 days later than the Spanish birds.

passages.title: Marsh grazing
passages.text: In one salt marsh, ecologists fenced snails out of some plots of cordgrass and left other plots open. After a season, the fenced plots held dense cordgrass, while many open plots had been grazed bare. In a nearby marsh where snail-eating crabs are abundant, however, the open plots looked nearly identical to the fenced ones. These results suggest that ______

passages.title: Songbird pitch
passages.text: Ecologist Dara Mensah studies a songbird whose city populations sing at a higher pitch than its rural populations. Many researchers attribute the difference to traffic noise, which masks low-pitched sounds. Mensah instead hypothesizes that young birds simply learn the songs of the adults around them, and that the first birds to settle in the city happened to sing at a higher pitch.

passages.title: Late quartets
passages.text: Composer Lena Ostrova's early string quartets were praised for their dense counterpoint, with all four instruments carrying independent melodies at once. Her later quartets abandon that density, often giving a single melody to one instrument while the others hold long, quiet chords. Some critics have called this change a decline in ambition. Ostrova's sketchbooks, however, show that she revised these sparse passages more times than any of her earlier music.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: she weighs several possible explanations and openly acknowledges the limits of the surviving records
candidates.explanation: The study weighs several explanations and admits the limits of its evidence, which describes a careful, restrained approach: "measured."

A.rationale: "Strident" means loud and forceful, the opposite of careful weighing.

C.rationale: "Cursory" means hasty and superficial, but the study weighs several explanations.

D.rationale: "Dogmatic" means insisting on one view, but the study considers several and admits uncertainty.

hints: What does the colon tell you about the study's approach?
Which word describes careful, restrained judgment?
candidates.remember: The words after a colon define the blank.
candidates.revision_note: S002-01 resubmitted: relabelled medium after both blind solvers rated it easy (72%); content unchanged.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely view the evidence cited by the planners in Text 1?

choices.A: As showing that widening a highway makes congestion worse right away
choices.B: As showing that drivers generally prefer to avoid newly widened roads
choices.C: As unreliable data that were probably measured incorrectly
choices.D: As accurate but too short-term to show a lasting effect

candidates.evidence: travel times often improve at first, but within a few years the new lanes tend to fill
candidates.explanation: Text 1's evidence covers only the year after widening. Text 2 agrees that travel times often improve at first but says congestion returns within a few years. So the researchers would accept the evidence but judge it too short-term to support a lasting conclusion.

A.rationale: Text 2 says travel times improve at first, so it does not claim congestion worsens right away.

B.rationale: Neither text discusses whether drivers prefer or avoid widened roads; Text 2 says more people choose to drive.

C.rationale: Text 2 agrees that travel times often improve at first, so it does not dispute the data's accuracy.

hints: What time period does Text 1's evidence cover?
What does Text 2 say happens after that period?

strategy.explanation: Compare the time frames of the two texts.

candidates.remember: Short-term evidence may not show long-term effects.
candidates.revision_note: S002-03 resubmitted: choices rebalanced so the key is no longer the longest; relabelled medium.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's observation?

choices.A: Town B had the most visits in both years, while Town C had the fewest visits in both years.
choices.B: Town C's visits rose by the largest percentage, while Town B's visits rose by the largest number.
choices.C: Town A's visits rose by 3,000, while Town C's visits rose by 2,400, a smaller number.
choices.D: Town B's visits rose by the largest percentage, while Town A's visits rose by the largest number.

candidates.evidence: the town with the largest percentage increase in visits was not the town with the largest increase in the number of visits
candidates.explanation: Increases: A +3,000 (25%), B +4,500 (15%), C +2,400 (30%). Town C has the largest percentage increase, but Town B has the largest increase in number. B states exactly that contrast.

A.rationale: Total visits in each year say nothing about either kind of increase.

C.rationale: Both numbers are correct, but neither town named has both the largest percentage and largest number, and no percentage is given.

D.rationale: Town B's 15% is the smallest percentage increase, and Town A's 3,000 is less than Town B's 4,500.

hints: Compute each town's increase in number and as a percent of its 2019 visits.
Check both halves of each choice against your numbers.

strategy.explanation: Check each half of each comparison against the computed increases.

candidates.remember: Percent change and absolute change can rank differently.
candidates.revision_note: S002-05 resubmitted: every choice is now a two-part comparison of similar length, and D is a near-miss that swaps the measures; relabelled medium.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: a set of bronze navigational dividers
candidates.explanation: The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. The subject is "a set," which is singular, and the narrative is in the past tense, so the verb is "was."

A.rationale: "Were" agrees with the nearby plural "objects" or "dividers," but the subject is the singular "a set."

C.rationale: "Are" is plural and also shifts out of the past tense.

D.rationale: "Have been" is plural and does not agree with "a set."

hints: Find the subject: it comes after the blank.
Is the head noun "set" or "dividers"?

strategy.explanation: Flip the sentence: "a set ... ______ among the objects."

candidates.remember: In inverted sentences, find the subject after the verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: had expected the cables to be the costliest part
candidates.explanation: Two independent clauses meet at the blank, so they need a semicolon (or period). "However" marks the contrast between what the committee expected and what happened, so it begins the second clause: "; however, the."

A.rationale: Commas alone join two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

B.rationale: This attaches "however" to the first clause, where nothing earlier is being contrasted; the contrast is with the anchorages' cost.

C.rationale: With no punctuation before "however," the two clauses run together.

hints: Are there complete sentences on both sides of the blank?
Which clause does "however" contrast with what came before?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate comma splices, then place "however" with the clause it contrasts.

candidates.remember: Semicolon before however when it starts a new clause.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.B: the paintings by Ines Varga recorded
choices.D: there were recorded by Ines Varga

candidates.evidence: Trained as a botanist before she turned to illustration
candidates.explanation: The opening phrase describes a person who was trained as a botanist, so the subject that follows it must be that person: "Ines Varga recorded."

A.rationale: The subject is "paintings," so the sentence says the paintings were trained as a botanist.

B.rationale: The subject is still "the paintings," which cannot have been trained as a botanist.

D.rationale: "There" leaves the opening phrase with nothing to modify and creates an awkward passive construction.

hints: Who was trained as a botanist?
Which choice puts that person right after the comma?

strategy.explanation: Ask who or what the opening phrase describes.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier must describe the subject that follows it.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: Using less steel would normally lower the cost, but the bridge will cost more anyway. "Even so" signals a result that holds despite the preceding fact.

A.rationale: Higher cost is not a consequence of using less steel; the text gives a different reason (individual fabrication).

C.rationale: The second sentence does not restate the first; it adds a contrasting fact.

D.rationale: "Likewise" signals a similar point, but higher cost contrasts with lower steel use.

hints: What would you expect less steel to do to the cost?
Does the second sentence meet or defy that expectation?
candidates.remember: A surprising result after a fact calls for a concession transition.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize that the Norwegian birds' earlier departure did not allow them to arrive first. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Although the Norwegian birds left West Africa about 9 days before the Spanish birds, they arrived about 11 days later.
choices.B: Both populations of the songbird winter in West Africa, but the Norwegian birds nest much farther north than the Spanish birds.
choices.C: The Norwegian birds reached their nesting grounds about 11 days after the Spanish birds, a sizable gap in arrival.
choices.D: The Norwegian birds left West Africa about 9 days ahead of the Spanish birds, giving them a head start on the trip north.

candidates.evidence: left West Africa an average of 9 days earlier
candidates.explanation: The goal pairs two facts: the earlier departure and the later arrival. Only A states both and links them with "Although" to stress the contrast.

B.rationale: This gives location facts but mentions neither the departure nor the arrival dates.

C.rationale: This gives the later arrival but omits the earlier departure, so the contrast is lost.

D.rationale: This gives the head start but not the later arrival, so it does not show that the head start failed.

hints: The goal has two parts: earlier departure and later arrival.
Which choice includes both?

strategy.explanation: Turn the goal into a checklist, then test each choice.

candidates.remember: Synthesis answers must meet every part of the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: snail grazing harms cordgrass mainly where predators do not keep snail numbers low.
choices.B: crabs harm cordgrass less than snails do, so marshes with crabs have denser cordgrass.
choices.C: fences protect cordgrass more effectively in marshes where snail-eating crabs are abundant.
choices.D: snails stop feeding on cordgrass entirely whenever crabs are present anywhere in a marsh.

candidates.evidence: where snail-eating crabs are abundant, however, the open plots looked nearly identical to the fenced ones
candidates.explanation: Without crabs, unprotected cordgrass was grazed bare; with abundant snail-eating crabs, unprotected cordgrass did as well as fenced cordgrass. So the snails' damage depends on whether predators keep their numbers down.

B.rationale: The text never says crabs eat or harm cordgrass; it describes them as eating snails.

C.rationale: In the crab marsh, fenced and open plots were nearly identical, so fences made little difference there.

D.rationale: "Stop ... entirely" goes beyond the data; the text supports fewer snails, not a total change in feeding.

hints: Compare open plots in the two marshes.
What is different about the second marsh?

strategy.explanation: Predict: grazing matters only where crabs are scarce.

candidates.remember: Look for what changes between the two conditions.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (weaken a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Mensah's hypothesis?

choices.A: Young birds raised in a quiet laboratory by rural adults sing at about the same pitch as rural birds.
choices.B: Rural birds that move into the city as adults continue to sing at their original lower pitch.
choices.C: Young birds raised in a quiet laboratory by city adults sing at a lower pitch than city birds do.
choices.D: City birds sing most often in the early morning, when traffic noise in the city is at its lowest.

candidates.evidence: young birds simply learn the songs of the adults around them
candidates.explanation: If pitch is learned, chicks raised by city adults should copy the high city pitch even in quiet. If they sing lower in a quiet lab, pitch tracks noise rather than learning, which undercuts Mensah.

A.rationale: Copying rural tutors is exactly what the learning hypothesis predicts (and the quiet lab fits the noise view too), so this does not weaken Mensah.

B.rationale: Adults that do not shift pitch in noisy cities fit Mensah's view and count against the noise explanation.

D.rationale: When birds sing most often does not show whether pitch is learned or caused by noise.

hints: What does each explanation predict for a chick raised in quiet by city adults?
Which finding fits the noise explanation but not learning?

strategy.explanation: For each finding, ask which hypothesis it fits; keep the one that fits only the rival.

candidates.remember: To weaken a claim, find a result it predicts wrongly.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the last sentence in the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains why Ostrova gave up the dense counterpoint of her early quartets.
choices.B: It suggests that the critics were right to prefer Ostrova's early quartets.
choices.C: It describes a technique Ostrova used in both her early and later quartets.
choices.D: It offers evidence that calls into question the critics' view of the change.

candidates.evidence: she revised these sparse passages more times than any of her earlier music
candidates.explanation: Critics call the later style a decline in ambition; the last sentence, introduced by "however," shows Ostrova worked harder on the sparse passages than on anything earlier, which challenges that view.

A.rationale: The sentence shows how much she revised, not why she changed styles.

B.rationale: "However" signals that the sentence pushes against the critics, not that it supports them.

C.rationale: The sentence concerns revising the later sparse passages, not a shared technique.

hints: What claim comes right before the last sentence?
What does "however" tell you about the last sentence's relation to it?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence before it and note the contrast word.

candidates.remember: A 'however' sentence after a claim usually challenges that claim.
